newsitem.title: USA: Superfund reforms save millions in cleanup costs.
newsitem.headline: Superfund reforms save millions in cleanup costs.

text.p: Companies have saved millions of dollars under reforms by the Environmental Protection Agency to ease cleanup standards at some Superfund toxic waste sites, a chemical industry group said Monday.
By EPA's own estimate, revisions in cleanup decisions at 37 sites resulted in savings of $285 million.

"The reforms are producing real benefits at real Superfund sites," said Mike Steinberg, an attorney with Morgan, Lewis and Bockius LLP, which did a survey of EPA offices and the industry for the Chemical Manufacturers Association.
But officials at the association said the reforms needed to be expanded, and the multibillion dollar program still had problems which could only be resolved by Congress.

According to survey responses from 70 companies involved in about half of the nation's 1,210 Superfund sites, changes in remedy standards over the last year led to savings of anywhere from zero to $82 million.

The survey focused on three changes by EPA which were designed to cut cleanup costs without sacrificing health and environmental protections, and two changes designed to divide costs more fairly among parties who polluted a singled site.
EPA officials criticized the report because, for reasons of confidentiality, companies which responded to the survey were not named.

"This methodology resulted in a good deal of information which we found to be unverifiable because it was not attributed to specific sites," EPA Superfund directors Stephen Luftig and Barry Breen said in a letter to CMA commenting on the report.
The agency has said its reforms should be used as a model for improving the Superfund law, which House and Senate lawmakers have been trying to overhaul over the last four years.
But Steinberg said at a news briefing, "Codifying the reforms is probably not the best way to get the program reformed."

Attempts to rewrite the law in the last two Congresses failed amid disagreements over how to shift more cleanup costs to the government, and who should be relieved from liability at sites where many parties dumped waste.
"My message (to Congress) would be 'Full speed ahead. Don't be slowed down by claims you sometimes hear that it's a fundamentally different program'," Steinberg said.

Senate lawmakers recently began talks with industry, environmental, and community officials on proposals for a new Superfund law, and aim to negotiate a bipartisan bill with the administration over the next month.
